lessons.title: Your Body Changes When You Move — Anchoring the Phenomenon

quiz.prompt: During the lesson, learners counted their pulse using the radial artery. Where should you place your fingers to find this pulse?
choices: Two fingers on the outside of the elbow
One hand flat on the chest, over the ribs
Two fingers (index and middle) on the inside of the wrist, below the thumb
Your thumb pressed hard on the side of the neck
quiz.rationale: The radial pulse is found with the index and middle fingers pressed gently on the inside of the wrist below the thumb. A flat hand on the chest was used for counting breaths, not pulse.
quiz.placement: Predict: counting resting pulse rate at the radial artery for 60 seconds

quiz.prompt: In a Grade 10 class, most learners had resting breathing rates between 12 and 20 breaths per minute and resting pulse rates between 60 and 90 beats per minute. Which pair of resting values fits this class pattern?
choices: 6 breaths per minute and 30 beats per minute
16 breaths per minute and 76 beats per minute
16 breaths per minute and 150 beats per minute
40 breaths per minute and 76 beats per minute
quiz.rationale: Only 16 breaths per minute and 76 beats per minute lie inside both class ranges (12–20 and 60–90). The other pairs have at least one value far outside the range.
quiz.placement: Predict: posting resting breathing and pulse rates on the class data table

quiz.prompt: Before exercise, a learner's resting pulse was 80 beats per minute. Immediately after 2 minutes of vigorous step-ups it was 128 beats per minute. By what percentage did the pulse rate increase?
quiz.rationale: Increase = 128 − 80 = 48 beats per minute. Percentage increase = 48 ÷ 80 × 100 = 60%. This is within the 50–80% rise seen in the class.
quiz.placement: Observe: 2 minutes of step-ups, then re-measuring pulse rate and comparing with the resting value

quiz.prompt: The class posted resting and post-exercise values for every learner on the board after the 2 minutes of step-ups. Which statement best describes the pattern in the whole-class data?
choices: Both rates rose for every learner, but by different amounts
Pulse rate rose for everyone, but breathing rate stayed the same
Breathing rate rose for everyone, but pulse rate stayed the same
Both rates rose by exactly the same amount for every learner
quiz.rationale: The class data showed that both breathing rate and pulse rate increased for everyone, which makes it a pattern. The size of the increase differed from learner to learner.
quiz.placement: Observe: whole-class data table analysis of resting and post-exercise values

quiz.prompt: Wanjiru predicted her breathing rate after the step-ups would be 26 breaths per minute. She then measured 30 breaths per minute. By how many breaths per minute was her prediction different from her measurement?
quiz.rationale: The difference between measured and predicted values is 30 − 26 = 4 breaths per minute, so her prediction was close.
quiz.placement: Explain: comparing written predictions with actual observations in groups of four

quiz.prompt: After the step-ups, some learners felt a burning sensation in their thigh muscles even though they were breathing hard the whole time. At this point in the unit, which statement is best supported by what the class has done so far?
choices: The burning only happens to learners who did not breathe hard
The burning proves that the heart is too weak to pump blood
The class has observed the burning but has not yet explained it, so it becomes a question to investigate
The burning has been proven to be caused by tired lungs
quiz.rationale: The class has only observed the burning sensation and has not yet gathered evidence to explain it. The sensible next step is to record it as a question on the Driving Question Board and investigate it in later lessons.
quiz.placement: Explain: groups propose explanations, which the teacher records without judgment (the BURNING clue)

quiz.prompt: Which of these would make the best question to post on the Driving Question Board after the step-ups activity?
choices: What colour sticky notes did we use?
What is the name of the wrist artery used for pulse?
How many learners are in our class?
Why did my legs burn even though I was breathing in plenty of air?
quiz.rationale: A good Driving Question Board question is a genuine 'Why' or 'How' question about the phenomenon, not a recall or routine question. Only the question about the burning legs asks about a puzzle the class observed.
quiz.placement: DQB: writing one 'biggest unanswered question' and posting it on the Driving Question Board

lessons.title: Characteristics of Respiratory Surfaces — What Makes a Good Gas Exchange Surface?

quiz.prompt: During step-ups your breathing rate doubled, so your lungs had to move twice as much oxygen into your blood in the same time. Which set of features would make a respiratory surface best at doing this job?
choices: Large surface area, thin wall, moist surface and a rich blood supply
Small surface area, thin wall, dry surface and a rich blood supply
Large surface area, thick wall, dry surface and a poor blood supply
Thick, hard wall with a small surface area and no blood supply
quiz.rationale: Gases diffuse quickly across a surface that is large, thin, moist and well supplied with blood. A thick, hard wall is a common misconception because it seems strong, but it slows diffusion.
quiz.placement: Predict: three features a respiratory surface must have (Our Predictions About Respiratory Surfaces)

quiz.prompt: An earthworm has no lungs or gills. How does it take in oxygen?
choices: Air enters through spiracles and travels along tracheal tubes
Oxygen diffuses through its thin, moist skin into the capillaries just beneath it
Air is breathed into millions of alveoli inside its body
Oxygen is taken from the water through gill lamellae
quiz.rationale: The earthworm uses cutaneous exchange. Its skin is thin and kept moist by mucus, with a capillary network below the epidermis, so oxygen diffuses straight in.
quiz.placement: Station A: Earthworm skin (cutaneous exchange)

quiz.prompt: A fish gill has many thin, plate-like lamellae on each gill filament. What is the main advantage of having so many lamellae?
choices: They make the wall thicker so less water enters the blood
They greatly increase the surface area for gas exchange
They make the gill hard and strong so it does not break
They keep the gill dry so oxygen can pass through
quiz.rationale: Many thin lamellae greatly increase the surface area in contact with water. More oxygen can diffuse into the blood at once.
quiz.placement: Station B: Fish gill lamellae

quiz.prompt: In an insect, oxygen enters through small openings called spiracles. How does the oxygen then reach the body cells?
choices: It diffuses through the insect's wet skin into the blood
It dissolves in water and passes over gill lamellae
Blood carries it from the lungs to the body cells
Tracheal tubes branch into tracheoles that carry air directly to the body cells
quiz.rationale: An insect's tracheal system delivers air through spiracles, tracheal tubes and tracheoles that end right next to body cells. Blood is not the main carrier of oxygen.
quiz.placement: Station C: Insect tracheal system

quiz.prompt: A teacher blows air from her lungs through a straw into clear limewater, and the limewater turns milky. What does this show?
choices: Exhaled air contains carbon dioxide
Exhaled air contains no gas, only water vapour
Exhaled air contains oxygen
Exhaled air contains nitrogen only
quiz.rationale: Limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide is present. This shows that CO₂ leaves the body in exhaled air, so gas exchange is happening.
quiz.placement: Whole-class limewater demonstration (between Station C and Station D)

quiz.prompt: The wall of an alveolus is only one cell thick. How does this help gas exchange?
choices: It makes the wall strong enough to pump gases into the blood
It keeps the alveolus dry so gases move faster
It shortens the distance gases must diffuse, so they cross quickly
It stores extra oxygen inside the wall
quiz.rationale: A very thin wall gives a short diffusion distance, so oxygen and carbon dioxide cross quickly. This is how breathing can double during exercise and still supply enough oxygen.
quiz.placement: Explain: master list 'Features of an Efficient Respiratory Surface' and connection paragraph

quiz.prompt: After a breath, oxygen is in the air inside the alveoli. Which statement gives the best partial answer to the question 'Where does the oxygen go once it enters the body?'
choices: The oxygen stays in the alveoli until we breathe out
The oxygen is changed into carbon dioxide inside the alveoli
The oxygen diffuses across the thin alveolar wall into the dense network of capillaries
The oxygen moves straight into the muscle cells through the lung wall
quiz.rationale: Evidence from the alveolus station shows a one-cell-thick wall and a dense capillary network. Oxygen diffuses from the alveolus into the blood, which then carries it away.
quiz.placement: DQB update: green sticky note partial answers

quiz.prompt: You add a zoom-in panel of an alveolus to your model, with arrows showing how gases move by diffusion. Which arrows are correct?
choices: Oxygen and carbon dioxide both move from the alveolus into the blood
Oxygen moves from the blood into the alveolus, and carbon dioxide moves from the alveolus into the blood
Oxygen moves from the alveolus into the blood, and carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the alveolus
Oxygen and carbon dioxide both move from the blood into the alveolus
quiz.rationale: Oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveolus into the blood. Carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveolus and is breathed out.
quiz.placement: Model: zoom-in alveolus panel added to the class model

lessons.title: Structure and Adaptations of Respiratory Surfaces

quiz.prompt: A student must pass oxygen across a surface as quickly as possible. She compares a smooth, flat, dry sheet of plastic with a crumpled, wet sponge. Which statement best explains why the crumpled, wet sponge is the better model of a gas-exchange surface?
choices: Surface area does not matter as long as the surface is thin
The folds give a much larger surface area, and the water film lets oxygen dissolve before it diffuses across
A dry surface lets oxygen pass through faster than a wet one
The sponge is heavier, so oxygen is pushed through it faster
quiz.rationale: Folding increases the area available for diffusion, and oxygen must dissolve in a moist film before crossing a surface. The flat dry plastic has neither feature.
quiz.placement: Predict: flat plastic sheet vs crumpled wet sponge, prediction journaling

quiz.prompt: In an insect, oxygen must reach the muscle cells. Which is the correct path that oxygen follows?
choices: Spiracle → tracheole → trachea → muscle cell
Spiracle → blood capillary → trachea → muscle cell
Spiracle → trachea → tracheole → muscle cell
Mouth → lungs → blood → muscle cell
quiz.rationale: Air enters through the spiracle, moves along the larger tracheae, and then into the narrow tracheoles that reach the cells directly. Insects do not use blood capillaries for oxygen transport.
quiz.placement: Station 3: Insect Tracheal System, tracing the path of oxygen from spiracle to muscle cell

quiz.prompt: The wall between the air in an alveolus and the blood in a capillary is about 0.2 micrometres thick. A sheet of paper is about 100 micrometres thick. How many times thinner is the alveolus wall than the paper?
choices: 50 times
20 times
5 000 times
500 times
quiz.rationale: Divide the paper thickness by the wall thickness: 100 ÷ 0.2 = 500, so the wall is 500 times thinner. This short distance lets oxygen diffuse across very quickly.
quiz.placement: Adaptation 2: Thin Walls (Short Diffusion Distance), comparing the alveolus wall with a sheet of paper

quiz.prompt: Why must the lining of the alveoli stay moist for gas exchange to work?
choices: Oxygen must dissolve in a film of water before it can diffuse across the membrane
Water in the alveoli carries oxygen around the body
Water makes the alveolus wall thicker so it does not tear
Moisture warms the air so that it moves faster
quiz.rationale: Gases cross the respiratory membrane when dissolved in a thin film of water. A dry surface would slow or stop diffusion.
quiz.placement: Adaptation 3: Moist Surface, discussion of what happens if the alveolus dried out

quiz.prompt: What is the main job of the dense network of blood capillaries around the alveoli in keeping gas exchange fast?
choices: It stores oxygen inside the alveolus until the body needs it
It carries oxygen away continuously, so the concentration gradient stays steep
It keeps the alveoli moist by releasing water into them
It makes the alveolus wall thicker and stronger
quiz.rationale: Flowing blood removes oxygen from the exchange surface, so the oxygen concentration in the alveolus stays higher than in the blood. This keeps the gradient steep and diffusion fast.
quiz.placement: Adaptation 4: Rich Blood Supply, concentration gradient and the 'team of buckets' analogy

quiz.prompt: After studying how oxygen crosses the alveoli into the blood, a class asks which part of the driving question is still NOT answered: 'Why does my body work so hard to get oxygen to cells during exercise, and what happens inside the cells when there is not enough?' Which question is still unanswered?
choices: What happens to the oxygen once it is inside the muscle cells?
How does oxygen dissolve in the moist lining of the alveolus?
Why do the alveoli have a large surface area?
Why are the alveolus walls thin?
quiz.rationale: The lesson explains how oxygen gets into the blood through the alveolus adaptations. What happens to oxygen inside the cells is left for later lessons on cellular respiration.
quiz.placement: DQB update: Answered Today, New Questions Raised and Model Connection (question mark after the arrow)

quiz.prompt: Humans, tilapia and insects have very different respiratory surfaces. Why do all efficient respiratory surfaces share the same adaptations of large surface area, thin walls and a moist surface?
choices: Because all animals live in water
Because large surface area and thin walls only matter for small animals
Because every animal breathes through lungs
Because all animals face the same problem of getting oxygen to their cells fast enough to release energy from food
quiz.rationale: Cells in all animals need oxygen to release energy from food, and diffusion is only fast enough with these features. This is the 'Big Idea' of the comparative model.
quiz.placement: Comparative Respiratory Surfaces three-panel model and 'Big Idea' sentence

quiz.prompt: A fisher at Kisumu finds that a tilapia has damaged gill lamellae, with many of the thin plates broken off. Why would this fish struggle to survive?
choices: Its blood becomes too thick to flow through the gills
It cannot swim, so water cannot reach its gills
Fewer lamellae mean less surface area, so it absorbs less dissolved oxygen from the water
Its gills will become too dry for gas exchange
quiz.rationale: The many thin lamellae give the gills a large surface area for taking oxygen from water, which holds little dissolved oxygen. Losing lamellae reduces the oxygen absorbed, so the fish cannot meet its needs.
quiz.placement: Exit task: explaining to a fisherman at Kisumu market why a tilapia with damaged gill lamellae would struggle

lessons.title: Mechanisms of Gaseous Exchange in Humans — External Respiration

quiz.prompt: In a side-view drawing of the human chest, where is the diaphragm found?
choices: At the throat, at the top of the windpipe
Between the two lungs, around the heart
Along the inside of the ribs, between neighbouring ribs
Just below the lungs, separating the chest from the abdomen
quiz.rationale: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle below the lungs and above the abdomen. Drawing it at the throat is a common misconception.
quiz.placement: Predict: sketch of the chest outline, marking where the diaphragm sits

quiz.prompt: What does the diaphragm do when you breathe IN (inhalation)?
choices: It stays still while only the ribs move
It relaxes and moves upward
It contracts and moves upward
It contracts and flattens, moving downward
quiz.rationale: During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens, moving down. This increases the volume of the thoracic cavity.
quiz.placement: Observe: animation, diaphragm row of the observation table (Timestamp 1)

quiz.prompt: During inhalation, what do the external intercostal muscles do, and what is the effect on the chest?
choices: They relax, so the ribs rise and the chest becomes bigger
They contract and pull the ribs inward and downward, making the chest smaller
They contract and raise the ribs upward and outward, making the chest bigger
They relax, so the ribs drop and the chest becomes smaller
quiz.rationale: Contraction of the external intercostal muscles lifts the rib cage upward and outward. This adds to the increase in thoracic volume caused by the diaphragm.
quiz.placement: Observe: animation, intercostal muscles row of the observation table (Timestamp 2)

quiz.prompt: When the volume of the thoracic cavity increases during inhalation, what happens to the air pressure inside the lungs, and why does air move in?
choices: Pressure falls, but air flows out because the lungs are now emptier
Pressure stays the same, and the lungs pull air in by themselves
Pressure falls slightly below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in from outside
Pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, so air is pushed into the lungs
quiz.rationale: A larger volume gives a lower pressure. Air moves from the higher atmospheric pressure to the slightly lower pressure in the lungs. The difference is small (about 0.1 kPa in quiet breathing) but enough to move air.
quiz.placement: Observe: animation, pressure-volume graph (Timestamp 3)

quiz.prompt: What is the pleural cavity?
choices: The fluid-filled space between the lung and the chest wall, which makes the lungs follow the chest's movements
The muscular space between the stomach and the diaphragm
The air space inside the lungs where gases are exchanged
The tube that carries air from the nose to the lungs
quiz.rationale: The pleural cavity is a fluid-filled space between the visceral and parietal pleura. It transmits pressure changes so the lungs follow the chest wall.
quiz.placement: Observe: animation, labelled sequence naming the pleural cavity and pleural fluid

quiz.prompt: In a bottle model of breathing, a balloon is stretched over the cut base of the bottle, and two small balloons hang inside on a Y-shaped straw open to the outside air. You pull the base balloon downward and the small balloons inflate. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Pulling the base balloon down increases the volume inside the bottle, so the pressure falls below the outside air pressure and air flows into the small balloons
The small balloons stretch and pull the air in by themselves
Pulling the base balloon down increases the pressure inside the bottle, which pushes air into the small balloons
Pulling the base balloon pushes extra air into the bottle, which fills the small balloons
quiz.rationale: Pulling the base down increases the volume around the small balloons and lowers the pressure there. The higher outside air pressure then pushes air in through the straw, as in the diaphragm flattening in the chest.
quiz.placement: Explain: improvised bell-jar diaphragm model, scaffold questions Q1 and Q2 (pulling the base balloon down)

quiz.prompt: After 2 minutes of step-ups your breathing rate doubled. What mainly makes your breathing speed up?
choices: The diaphragm contracts and relaxes on its own without any signals from the brain
Your blood runs out of nitrogen, so the brain tells the lungs to take in more
The lungs get tired, so they pull in air more quickly by themselves
Your muscles make more carbon dioxide, which makes the blood slightly more acidic, so the breathing centre in the brain sends faster signals to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles
quiz.rationale: Exercising muscles produce more carbon dioxide. Sensors detect the change, and the breathing centre (medulla) sends faster signals to the breathing muscles. The lungs do not pull air in by themselves.
quiz.placement: DQB: teacher input answering 'What makes a breath happen — is it automatic?'

lessons.title: Mechanisms of Gaseous Exchange in Humans — Alveolar & Cellular Exchange

quiz.prompt: Oxygen moves from the air in the alveolus into the blood in the surrounding capillary. What makes oxygen move in this direction?
choices: Red blood cells push oxygen across the alveolar wall using energy
The heart sucks oxygen out of the alveolus into the blood
Oxygen moves from low concentration to high concentration so that the blood fills up
Oxygen diffuses from a higher concentration in the alveolus to a lower concentration in the blood
quiz.rationale: Blood arriving at the lungs has less oxygen than the air in the alveolus, so oxygen diffuses down its concentration gradient from high to low. No pump or push is needed at this step.
quiz.placement: Oxygen Journey table: Alveolus row (Direction of diffusion column)

quiz.prompt: After oxygen crosses into the lung capillary, which part of the blood mainly carries it around the body?
choices: Haemoglobin inside red blood cells, forming oxyhaemoglobin
Plasma alone, with no help from any cells
Platelets, which seal wounds
White blood cells, which fight germs
quiz.rationale: Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin, which is how most oxygen is transported. Naming haemoglobin or red blood cells is more precise than just saying 'blood'.
quiz.placement: Oxygen Journey table: Lung capillary row (What carries O₂? column)

quiz.prompt: Which list shows the correct route of oxygen-rich blood after it leaves the lungs, until it reaches the capillaries in a leg muscle?
choices: Pulmonary vein → left side of the heart → aorta → arteries → muscle capillaries
Pulmonary vein → right side of the heart → vena cava → muscle capillaries
Pulmonary artery → left side of the heart → aorta → muscle capillaries
Lung capillaries → straight to muscle capillaries, without passing through the heart
quiz.rationale: Oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs in the pulmonary vein to the left side of the heart. The heart pumps it into the aorta and arteries, which lead to the muscle capillaries. The heart is a pump on the route, not the final destination.
quiz.placement: Reading: route of oxygenated blood (Oxygen Journey table: Heart row)

quiz.prompt: In the muscle, oxygen leaves the blood in the capillaries and enters the muscle cells. Why does oxygen move into the muscle cells?
choices: Haemoglobin stays in the capillary and forces oxygen out with the blood pressure
Muscle cells use up oxygen in respiration, so there is less oxygen inside them than in the blood, and oxygen diffuses in down the concentration gradient
The heart pushes oxygen directly through the cell membrane of each muscle cell
Muscle cells have more oxygen than the blood, so oxygen is pulled in by the high concentration inside the cell
quiz.rationale: Working muscle cells use oxygen for respiration, so the oxygen concentration inside them stays lower than in the capillary blood. Oxygen therefore diffuses from the blood into the cells.
quiz.placement: Molecule Narration: the oxygen molecule enters the muscle cell

quiz.prompt: Achieng's pulse rose from 74 to 128 beats per minute after step-ups. Which claim and reasoning best explain why her heart beat faster?
choices: The heart beats faster so that haemoglobin carries more oxygen to the muscles each minute, because the muscles are using oxygen faster
The heart beats faster to make more oxygen for the muscles to use
The heart beats faster so that the lungs can stop working and rest during exercise
The heart beats faster so that oxygen can stay inside the heart until it is needed
quiz.rationale: Haemoglobin in red blood cells carries oxygen, so more heartbeats per minute means more oxygen delivered per minute to muscles that are using it faster. The heart pumps oxygen but does not make it or store it.
quiz.placement: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning card on the Driving Question Board: 'Why does the heart beat faster?'

quiz.prompt: Muscle cells that are working hard produce carbon dioxide. What happens to this carbon dioxide?
choices: It diffuses from the muscle cells into the blood and is carried back to the lungs to be breathed out
It is carried by the heart straight out of the body through the skin
It turns into oxygen inside the red blood cells
It stays in the muscle cells until the exercise ends
quiz.rationale: Carbon dioxide is at a higher concentration in the muscle cells than in the blood, so it diffuses into the capillaries. The blood carries it to the lungs, the reverse of the oxygen route, and it leaves the body when we breathe out.
quiz.placement: Oxygen Journey table: CO₂ diffusion back into the blood and transport to the lungs (extension in the Model phase)

quiz.prompt: In a diagram of the circulatory system, oxygen-poor blood is usually drawn blue and oxygen-rich blood red. What is the colour of real oxygen-poor blood inside the body?
choices: Bright red
Dark red
Bright blue
Purple-green
quiz.rationale: Blue is only a colour code used in diagrams. Real oxygen-poor blood is dark red, and veins only look blue through the skin.
quiz.placement: Cumulative model revision: colour code for oxygenated (red) and deoxygenated (blue) blood

lessons.title: Aerobic Respiration: Unlocking Energy from Ugali Inside Your Cells

quiz.prompt: Which word equation correctly shows aerobic respiration in a muscle cell?
choices: ATP + oxygen → glucose + carbon dioxide + water
glucose + carbon dioxide → oxygen + water + ATP
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + ATP
oxygen + water → glucose + carbon dioxide + ATP
quiz.rationale: Glucose and oxygen are the reactants. Carbon dioxide, water and ATP (energy) are the products.
quiz.placement: Step 1 (Word Equation): glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP)

quiz.prompt: Mwangi's muscles use the balanced equation C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP. How many hydrogen atoms are in 6H₂O on the right-hand side?
quiz.rationale: Each H₂O has 2 hydrogen atoms, so 6 × 2 = 12 hydrogen atoms. This matches the 12 hydrogen atoms in C₆H₁₂O₆, so the equation is balanced for hydrogen.
quiz.placement: Step 2 (Balanced Chemical Equation): pair atom-counting of C, H and O

quiz.prompt: A learner annotates a diagram of a mitochondrion. Which set of arrows is correct for aerobic respiration?
choices: Glucose and oxygen enter; carbon dioxide, water and ATP leave or are made
ATP and oxygen enter; glucose and carbon dioxide leave
Only oxygen enters; only ATP leaves
Carbon dioxide and water enter; glucose and ATP leave
quiz.rationale: The reactants (glucose-derived fuel and oxygen) go in. The products (CO₂, H₂O and ATP) come out. ATP is made, not taken in.
quiz.placement: Step 3 (Mitochondrion Annotation): arrows for reactants entering and products leaving

quiz.prompt: Aerobic respiration has three stages. Which stage takes place in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondrion, and gives only 2 ATP per glucose?
choices: The Krebs cycle
The electron transport chain
Glycolysis
Breathing in
quiz.rationale: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, where glucose is split into pyruvate with a small yield of 2 ATP. The Krebs cycle and electron transport chain happen in the mitochondrion, where most ATP is made.
quiz.placement: Naming the three stages: glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain

quiz.prompt: A student says, "Oxygen is the energy that makes my muscles work." Which statement is the best correction?
choices: Oxygen is stored in muscles and used up first before any food is used.
Glucose is the fuel, and oxygen allows it to be fully broken down to release its energy as ATP.
Oxygen is turned into glucose, and glucose is the energy.
Oxygen is the fuel, and glucose only helps to carry it to the cells.
quiz.rationale: Glucose holds the chemical energy. Oxygen is the enabler that lets glucose be fully broken down so the energy is released as ATP.
quiz.placement: Teacher addresses the misconception 'Oxygen IS the energy' after the CER exercise

quiz.prompt: During 2 minutes of step-ups, Achieng's breathing rate rose from 16 to 34 breaths per minute and her pulse rose from 74 to 128 beats per minute. Which explanation best uses aerobic respiration?
choices: Her lungs needed to get bigger, so her heart beat faster to push them open.
Oxygen is the energy her muscles use directly, so she had to breathe more to store energy.
Her body made less carbon dioxide during exercise, so she breathed faster to get more of it.
Her muscle cells needed more ATP, and making ATP uses oxygen, so faster breathing and heartbeat bring oxygen in and carry carbon dioxide away.
quiz.rationale: More muscle contraction needs more ATP. Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen to make ATP and produces CO₂. Faster breathing and pulse deliver oxygen and remove CO₂.
quiz.placement: Claim–Evidence–Reasoning exercise about Achieng's breathing and pulse rates

quiz.prompt: Achieng felt a burning sensation in her legs even though she was breathing hard. The aerobic respiration equation assumes something that may not always be true during hard exercise. What is it?
choices: That muscle cells do not need ATP
That glucose is made inside the mitochondrion
That enough oxygen is always available to the muscle cells
That carbon dioxide is never produced
quiz.rationale: The equation for aerobic respiration only works when oxygen is available. The burning raises the new question of what happens when oxygen cannot keep up with ATP demand.
quiz.placement: New red DQB card: 'What happens when the oxygen supply cannot keep up with the ATP demand?'

quiz.prompt: In a model of a muscle cell, carbon dioxide leaves the mitochondrion. Which path should the model show for this carbon dioxide?
choices: It moves into the blood, then to the alveoli, and is exhaled.
It is turned back into glucose inside the muscle cell.
It stays in the mitochondrion until the muscle stops working.
It is used to make ATP, which leaves the cell.
quiz.rationale: CO₂ made in respiration diffuses from the cell into the blood. The blood carries it to the lungs, where it passes into the alveoli and is exhaled. This links to the rise in CO₂ during exercise.
quiz.placement: Adding the cellular layer to the cumulative model: CO₂ leaving the mitochondrion → blood → alveolus → exhaled

lessons.title: Anaerobic Respiration: Yeast Balloons, Burning Legs, and Oxygen Debt

quiz.prompt: A group mixes warm water, sugar and dried yeast in a bottle and stretches a balloon over the neck. After 10 minutes the balloon has started to inflate. Which gas is mainly inflating the balloon?
choices: Oxygen made by the yeast
Carbon dioxide produced by the yeast during respiration
Nitrogen released from the sugar
Ethanol vapour that is lighter than air
quiz.rationale: Yeast respire the sugar and release carbon dioxide gas, which collects in the balloon. Yeast do not produce oxygen, and the sugar does not release nitrogen.
quiz.placement: Yeast Balloon practical: monitoring balloon circumference every 5 minutes

quiz.prompt: A teacher wants to be sure that the CO₂ in a yeast balloon set-up comes from respiration WITHOUT oxygen. Which change to the set-up would help most?
choices: Add extra sugar and shake the bottle every minute
Remove the balloon so that air can enter the bottle
Use water that was boiled and cooled, and float a thin layer of cooking oil on top
Use much hotter water, about 80 °C, so the yeast work faster
quiz.rationale: Boiled and cooled water has little dissolved oxygen, and the oil layer stops new air from dissolving in. Hot water would kill the yeast, and shaking or removing the balloon adds oxygen.
quiz.placement: Yeast Balloon practical: teacher question 'Is there oxygen in this bottle? How could we make sure the CO₂ comes from respiration WITHOUT oxygen?'

quiz.prompt: Which equation correctly shows anaerobic respiration in yeast?
choices: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + energy
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy
C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ + energy
C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + energy
quiz.rationale: Yeast break glucose down without oxygen into ethanol and carbon dioxide, releasing a little energy. The equation has no oxygen on the left side, and 6 C, 12 H and 6 O are present on each side.
quiz.placement: Observation Sheet: writing the word and balanced chemical equations for aerobic and anaerobic respiration

quiz.prompt: During the final sprint of an 800 m race, a runner's muscle cells do not get enough oxygen. What does anaerobic respiration in these muscle cells produce?
choices: Lactic acid, with a small amount of energy
Lactic acid, carbon dioxide and water
Carbon dioxide and water, with a large amount of energy
Ethanol and carbon dioxide
quiz.rationale: In animal muscle cells, glucose is partly broken down without oxygen into lactic acid, releasing only a little energy (about 2 ATP). Ethanol and CO₂ is the yeast pathway, and CO₂ and water come from aerobic respiration.
quiz.placement: 'Burning legs' video clip: annotating what is happening in the runner's cells

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly compares aerobic respiration with anaerobic respiration in muscle cells?
choices: Aerobic respiration releases less energy because it uses oxygen up
Aerobic respiration releases much more energy from the same glucose because it breaks the glucose down completely
Anaerobic respiration releases more energy because it is faster
Both release the same amount of energy from one glucose molecule
quiz.rationale: With oxygen, glucose is broken down completely to CO₂ and water, releasing a lot of energy. Without oxygen, glucose is only partly broken down to lactic acid, so little energy is released.
quiz.placement: Whole-class side-by-side comparison table (Aerobic, Anaerobic animals, Anaerobic yeast)

quiz.prompt: A learner writes an explanation of why lactic acid builds up in leg muscles during intense step-ups. Which explanation is scientifically correct?
choices: Oxygen reaches the muscle cells more slowly than they need it, so some glucose is broken down without oxygen and forms lactic acid
Extra carbon dioxide in the blood is changed into lactic acid
Oxygen is poisonous to muscles, so lactic acid is made to get rid of it
The muscles run out of glucose, so they make lactic acid from fat
quiz.rationale: When the oxygen supply cannot meet the demand of working muscles, glucose is partly broken down by anaerobic respiration, and lactic acid is the product. Lactic acid is not made from fat or CO₂, and oxygen is not toxic to muscles.
quiz.placement: Individual structured written explanation: why lactic acid builds up in leg muscles during intense step-ups

quiz.prompt: After a hard race, an athlete keeps breathing deeply and quickly for several minutes. Which statement best explains this using the idea of oxygen debt?
choices: The athlete needs extra oxygen to break down the lactic acid that built up during the race
The athlete's lungs have been damaged by the lactic acid
The athlete is breathing out the ethanol made during the race
The athlete is removing the extra oxygen stored in the muscles
quiz.rationale: Oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down the accumulated lactic acid. Deep breathing after the race supplies this oxygen. Ethanol is made by yeast, not by human muscles.
quiz.placement: Cumulative 'Body During Exercise' model revision: sentence defining oxygen debt

lessons.title: Respiratory Quotient (RQ): What Fuel Is Your Body Burning?

quiz.prompt: Respiratory Quotient (RQ) is used to tell what fuel the body is burning. Which formula gives RQ?
choices: RQ = CO₂ produced × O₂ consumed
RQ = CO₂ produced − O₂ consumed
RQ = CO₂ produced ÷ O₂ consumed
RQ = O₂ consumed ÷ CO₂ produced
quiz.rationale: RQ is the ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen consumed, with CO₂ on top. Inverting the ratio (O₂ ÷ CO₂) is the common error.
quiz.placement: Observe: structured reading 'Measuring the Body's Fuel Gauge' (definition of RQ and its formula)

quiz.prompt: Three foods are eaten in Kenya: ugali (maize starch), nyama choma (fat-rich meat) and githeri (beans and maize, mainly protein and carbohydrate). When each is respired, which food gives the LOWEST RQ?
choices: All three have the same RQ because all use oxygen
Githeri, with an RQ of about 0.9
Nyama choma, with an RQ of about 0.7
Ugali, with an RQ of about 1.0
quiz.rationale: Fat has the lowest RQ (about 0.7). Carbohydrate is about 1.0 and protein about 0.9, so the foods give different RQ values.
quiz.placement: Observe: mini-lecture on ugali, nyama choma and githeri RQ values ('What pattern do you notice about which food has the lowest RQ?')

quiz.prompt: A Kericho tea-farm worker doing light weeding consumes 500 mL of O₂ and produces 350 mL of CO₂ per minute. What is the worker's RQ?
quiz.rationale: RQ = CO₂ produced ÷ O₂ consumed = 350 ÷ 500 = 0.7. The value 1.43 comes from inverting the ratio.
quiz.placement: Explain: Problem 2 (guided) – tea-farm worker doing light weeding

quiz.prompt: A long-distance runner training in Iten consumes 2,000 mL of O₂ and produces 1,900 mL of CO₂ per minute. What is the runner's RQ, and which fuel is mainly being respired?
choices: 0.95, mainly carbohydrate
0.95, mainly fat
0.70, mainly fat
1.05, mainly carbohydrate
quiz.rationale: RQ = 1,900 ÷ 2,000 = 0.95. This is close to 1.0, so the runner is mainly respiring carbohydrate, like ugali. A fat-dominated RQ would be near 0.7.
quiz.placement: Explain: Problem 3 (independent) – long-distance runner from Iten

quiz.prompt: At the start of the Nairobi Marathon a runner's RQ is 0.97. By the 30 km mark it has dropped to 0.85. What does this change show?
choices: The runner is using less oxygen than at the start, so the body has relaxed
The runner is using more fat as fuel than at the start, so the fuel is a mixture
The runner is now using only carbohydrate
The runner has stopped respiring and is now using only protein
quiz.rationale: An RQ falling from near 1.0 towards 0.7 means the fuel is shifting from carbohydrate towards fat. An RQ of 0.85 shows a mixture of fuels.
quiz.placement: Explain: Problem 4 (extension/discussion) – Nairobi Marathon RQ 0.97 to 0.85

quiz.prompt: During a long run, a muscle cell uses more fat and less carbohydrate, so its RQ falls. What does this change mean for the cell's oxygen needs?
choices: The cell needs no O₂ at all because fat is burned anaerobically
The cell needs slightly more O₂ for the same amount of energy, on top of the large rise in total energy demand
The cell needs exactly the same O₂ as with carbohydrate
The cell needs much less O₂, so breathing can slow down
quiz.rationale: Fat needs slightly more oxygen per unit of energy (roughly 5 to 10% more) than carbohydrate. This is a small extra on top of the large rise in total energy demand, so the lungs and heart keep working hard.
quiz.placement: DQB: teacher links new RQ notes to breathing rate and oxygen demand with red-marker arrows

quiz.prompt: After 2 minutes of hard step-ups, a learner feels a burning sensation in the leg muscles. What explains this burning?
choices: Lactic acid made by anaerobic respiration in the muscles
Too much O₂ entering the muscle cells
Fat being burned, which always causes the burning feeling
The RQ rising above 1.0 and damaging the muscle
quiz.rationale: The burning comes from lactic acid made by anaerobic respiration, as learned in Lesson 7. The fuel switch from carbohydrate towards fat is a different change, seen in long exercise such as a marathon.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the RQ layer to the cumulative explanatory model (link back to the burning in the legs during the step-ups)

lessons.title: Practical & Data Analysis: Factors Affecting the Rate of Respiration

quiz.prompt: In an investigation, groups place the same yeast–glucose suspension in water baths at 10 °C, 25 °C, 37 °C and 50 °C and count the bubbles of carbon dioxide produced each minute. What is the independent variable?
choices: The time for which bubbles are counted
The volume of yeast–glucose suspension
The temperature of the water bath
The number of CO₂ bubbles counted per minute
quiz.rationale: The independent variable is the one the investigator deliberately changes. Here it is the water bath temperature. The bubble count is the dependent variable, and volume and time are controlled.
quiz.placement: Observe: teacher asks 'What type of variable is temperature in our experiment?'

quiz.prompt: In the yeast experiment, only temperature is meant to change between groups. Which of these must be kept the SAME in every group so the test is fair?
choices: The number of bubbles counted
The rate of CO₂ production
The volume of the yeast–glucose suspension (10 mL)
The temperature of the water bath
quiz.rationale: Control variables such as the volume and concentration of the suspension and the counting time must be kept constant. Temperature is the variable being changed, and bubbles or rate are the results being measured.
quiz.placement: Observe: groups set up boiling tubes with 10 mL of 5% glucose–yeast suspension

quiz.prompt: A group at the 37 °C station counts CO₂ bubbles for three successive minutes and gets 18, 20 and 22 bubbles per minute. What mean value should the group enter in the class data table?
choices: 18 bubbles per minute
22 bubbles per minute
20 bubbles per minute
60 bubbles per minute
quiz.rationale: The mean is the total of the three readings divided by 3. (18 + 20 + 22) ÷ 3 = 60 ÷ 3 = 20 bubbles per minute.
quiz.placement: Observe: each group records three readings and enters its mean in the class data table

quiz.prompt: The class data shows that the yeast produces much less CO₂ at 50 °C than at 37 °C. What is the best explanation?
choices: The glucose was all used up in the first minute at 50 °C
The enzymes at 50 °C are used up because they work too fast
The enzymes that control respiration lose their shape (denature) at the high temperature and can no longer work properly
The yeast respires faster at 50 °C but the CO₂ cannot escape
quiz.rationale: Respiration is controlled by enzymes, which are proteins. Above the optimum temperature they change shape (denature), so they stop working and the rate falls.
quiz.placement: Explain: structured question 2 – Why does the rate fall sharply between 37 °C and 50 °C?

quiz.prompt: A learner plots the mean CO₂ production rate of yeast at 10 °C, 25 °C, 37 °C and 50 °C. Which description matches the pattern the class results should show?
choices: The rate stays the same at all four temperatures
The rate rises steadily and is highest at 50 °C
The rate is highest at 10 °C and falls as temperature rises
The rate rises from 10 °C to a highest value at about 37 °C, then falls at 50 °C
quiz.rationale: Enzyme-controlled reactions speed up as temperature rises towards the optimum (about 37 °C). Above the optimum the enzymes denature and the rate drops, which gives a rise then a fall.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the temperature–rate curve ('enzyme-controlled; optimum ~37 °C') to the cellular respiration diagram

quiz.prompt: After 2 minutes of step-ups, a learner's skin feels warm. Which statement best explains why body temperature rises during exercise?
choices: Oxygen is a hot gas that warms the muscles when it arrives
Breathing faster pushes warm air into the blood
The enzymes in the muscles denature and give out heat
Cellular respiration in the muscle cells releases heat as a by-product
quiz.rationale: Cellular respiration releases energy, and some of it escapes as heat. When muscles respire faster during exercise, more heat is released and body temperature rises.
quiz.placement: Explain: structured question 3 – connecting the data to the warmth felt after step-ups

quiz.prompt: An athlete training in Iten gets very hot, and body temperature rises to about 39–40 °C. Human enzymes denature at about 45 °C and above. Why do the athlete's respiration enzymes not denature?
choices: Enzymes in athletes cannot denature
Body temperature rises to 50 °C but the enzymes only denature in yeast
Sweating and blood flow to the skin carry heat away, and the body temperature stays below the temperature at which enzymes denature
The enzymes stop working during exercise so heat cannot harm them
quiz.rationale: Body temperature rises only a few degrees in hard exercise, which is below the denaturing temperature. Sweating and skin blood flow remove the extra heat.
quiz.placement: DQB: 'Still Wondering' card about Iten athletes and enzyme denaturation

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Rate of Respiration (continued) & Importance of Gaseous Exchange

quiz.prompt: Achieng ate a large plate of ugali and githeri before a race, so her muscles have plenty of glucose. In a yeast experiment, the rate of CO₂ production rose as glucose concentration increased, then levelled off (plateau) at high glucose concentrations. What does the plateau show?
choices: The yeast cells stopped respiring because the glucose was used up
Adding more glucose always makes respiration faster
Glucose is no longer needed for respiration at high concentrations
Enzymes are working at their maximum rate, so extra glucose cannot speed up respiration
quiz.rationale: At the plateau the enzyme active sites are saturated, so more substrate cannot increase the rate. The common misconception is that more glucose always means faster energy release.
quiz.placement: Scenario A: Achieng, ugali and githeri before the 400 m race

quiz.prompt: Kamau farms at 2,400 m in the Rift Valley, where the air has 21% oxygen but lower air pressure. A farmer in Mombasa does the same task at sea level. Which prediction is best?
choices: Kamau's cells get less oxygen per breath, so his maximum aerobic respiration rate is lower
Kamau's aerobic respiration rate is higher because the air is thinner
Altitude has no effect on respiration because only glucose matters
Kamau's cells get the same oxygen per breath because the air is still 21% oxygen
quiz.rationale: Lower air pressure means each breath delivers fewer oxygen molecules even though the percentage is the same, so less oxygen reaches the cells for aerobic respiration.
quiz.placement: Scenario B: Kamau, maize farmer at 2,400 m altitude

quiz.prompt: Kenyan long-distance runners were tested at Nairobi (1,795 m), Eldoret (2,085 m) and a camp near Mt. Kenya (3,000 m). Their maximum aerobic respiration rate (VO₂ max) decreased as altitude increased. Which statement correctly DESCRIBES the pattern without explaining it?
choices: Respiration rate falls because each breath delivers fewer oxygen molecules
Runners at high altitude have damaged lungs, so their respiration rate falls
Maximum aerobic respiration rate falls as altitude rises
The runners at 3,000 m used more glucose, so the rate fell
quiz.rationale: A description states only the pattern in the data (rate decreases as altitude increases). The other options give explanations or unsupported claims, which belong to the explain phase.
quiz.placement: Graph 2: VO₂ max of Kenyan long-distance runners at different altitudes (DESCRIBE prompt)

quiz.prompt: In a yeast experiment, glucose concentrations of 0%, 2%, 5%, 10% and 20% were used and CO₂ production was measured. Which variable is the factor affecting respiration, and which is the measure of respiration rate?
choices: Factor: CO₂ production; measure: glucose concentration
Factor: glucose concentration; measure: CO₂ production
Factor: CO₂ production; measure: time of day
Factor: yeast; measure: glucose concentration
quiz.rationale: Glucose concentration (substrate) is the variable changed, so it is on the x-axis. CO₂ production is the response that shows the rate of respiration. Mixing these up is a common graph-reading error.
quiz.placement: Graph 1: Substrate concentration vs. rate of CO₂ production in yeast (IDENTIFY prompt)

quiz.prompt: Why does lower oxygen availability reduce the rate of aerobic respiration?
choices: Oxygen is the substrate that is broken down to release energy
Oxygen makes enzymes of glycolysis denature
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain, so less oxygen slows ATP production
Oxygen is only needed to remove lactic acid after exercise
quiz.rationale: Without enough O₂ the electron transport chain slows and less ATP is made, so cells rely more on anaerobic respiration. Oxygen is not the substrate; glucose is.
quiz.placement: Part A: CER discussion on oxygen availability (Graph 2)

quiz.prompt: After 2 minutes of step-ups, a learner breathes hard but still feels a burning sensation in the leg muscles. What is the best explanation?
choices: The muscles have run out of glucose completely
Breathing hard damages the lungs and causes burning in the legs
Too much oxygen has reached the muscles and burned them
Oxygen delivery to the muscle cells is not fast enough, so some anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid
quiz.rationale: When oxygen supply to muscle cells cannot keep up with demand, cells use anaerobic respiration and lactic acid builds up, causing the burning feeling.
quiz.placement: Part A: CER discussion on oxygen availability, linking the burning sensation to the step-up data

quiz.prompt: A disease destroys alveoli and reduces the respiratory surface area of a person's lungs from 70 m² to 30 m². According to the idea that diffusion rate is proportional to surface area, what happens?
choices: More oxygen diffuses into the blood per breath
Carbon dioxide is no longer produced by the cells
Less oxygen diffuses into the blood, so the maximum aerobic respiration rate falls
Oxygen diffusion stays the same because breathing rate does not change
quiz.rationale: A smaller respiratory surface allows less oxygen to diffuse per unit time, which lowers the maximum rate of aerobic respiration, as in emphysema.
quiz.placement: Part A: CER discussion on surface area of respiratory membrane (Fick's Law)

quiz.prompt: A tea picker in Kericho works in the cold highlands and keeps her body temperature steady. Which life process that depends on energy from cellular respiration does this show?
choices: Active transport
Heat regulation
Reproduction
Growth
quiz.rationale: Energy released by respiration produces heat that helps maintain body temperature in cold conditions.
quiz.placement: Part B: concept map, HEAT REGULATION node with Kenyan example

quiz.prompt: Which example correctly shows ACTIVE TRANSPORT using energy from respiration?
choices: Absorption of glucose from digested githeri into the cells lining the small intestine against a concentration gradient
A runner's leg muscles contracting during a marathon
Water vapour leaving the body when breathing out
Oxygen diffusing from the alveoli into the blood
quiz.rationale: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient and needs ATP from respiration. Oxygen diffusion is passive; muscle contraction is movement.
quiz.placement: Part B: concept map, ACTIVE TRANSPORT node with Kenyan example

quiz.prompt: On a cumulative respiratory model, a learner adds the note: 'Rate decreases if O₂ falls, such as at high altitude, so less ATP is made, anaerobic respiration occurs and lactic acid causes burning.' Where should the arrow for this note point?
choices: The alveolar membrane
The glucose label in the blood
The windpipe
The electron transport chain section of the mitochondrion
quiz.rationale: Oxygen is used at the electron transport chain in the mitochondrion, so the oxygen-availability annotation belongs there. Surface area is annotated on the alveolar membrane.
quiz.placement: Cumulative model revision: annotation 2 (O₂ in blood to electron transport chain)

lessons.title: Model Building and Driving Question Board Consolidation

quiz.prompt: A learner's pulse rises from 72 to over 120 beats per minute and breathing rate doubles during 2 minutes of step-ups. Which explanation is the best one?
choices: Breathing and pulse rise because the lungs and heart become tired and work harder to keep going.
The heart beats faster to push air into the lungs, and breathing faster only cools the body.
The working muscles respire faster, so they need more oxygen and must lose more carbon dioxide. Faster breathing takes in oxygen and faster heartbeat carries it to the muscles.
The muscles stop respiring during exercise, so the body breathes faster to restart them.
quiz.rationale: Exercising muscle cells respire faster, so oxygen demand and carbon dioxide production rise. The lungs supply oxygen and the faster-beating heart transports it to the muscles in the blood.
quiz.placement: Predict phase: individual list of everything needed to explain why breathing rate doubled and pulse rose after the Lesson 1 step-up exercise

quiz.prompt: After step-ups, a learner's leg muscles feel a burning sensation even though the learner was breathing hard throughout. What is the best explanation?
choices: The muscles produced too much carbon dioxide, which is the same as lactic acid.
Breathing hard dried out the muscles, causing the burning feeling.
The muscle cells ran short of oxygen for their energy demand, so some glucose was broken down without oxygen to form lactic acid.
Too much oxygen reached the muscles and burned the muscle tissue.
quiz.rationale: When oxygen supply cannot meet demand, muscle cells use anaerobic respiration, which produces lactic acid and causes the burning feeling. This is why an exemplar model without the anaerobic pathway cannot explain burning legs.
quiz.placement: Observe phase: red-pen critique of the partially completed exemplar model (missing lactic acid pathway)

quiz.prompt: Fish gill lamellae, insect tracheoles and human alveoli all allow fast gas exchange. According to Fick's Law, which change to a respiratory surface would INCREASE the rate of diffusion of gases across it?
choices: Making the oxygen concentration equal on both sides of the surface
Reducing the surface area of the surface
Making the wall thicker for extra strength
Making the surface wall thinner so the diffusion distance is shorter
quiz.rationale: Diffusion is faster with a large surface area, a short diffusion distance (thin wall) and a steep concentration gradient. Only a thinner wall improves exchange.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: Zone A - Comparative Respiratory Surfaces (Fick's Law named in Zone A)

quiz.prompt: Which set of events correctly describes inhalation in humans?
choices: The diaphragm relaxes and domes upward, the ribs move down and in, the chest volume decreases and the pressure inside rises.
The diaphragm contracts and flattens, the ribs move down and in, the chest volume decreases and the pressure inside rises.
The intercostal muscles relax, the ribs move up and out, the chest volume increases and the pressure inside rises above atmospheric pressure.
The diaphragm contracts and flattens, the external intercostal muscles contract and move the ribs up and out, the chest volume increases and the pressure inside falls below atmospheric pressure.
quiz.rationale: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles increases thorax volume, lowering the pressure inside the lungs below the outside air pressure, so air flows in.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: Zone B - Human Breathing Mechanics (muscle names, rib movement, pressure change)

quiz.prompt: Which sequence correctly shows the pathway of oxygen from the air in the alveolus to the cells of an exercising muscle?
choices: It dissolves in the blood plasma, goes to the heart where it is used up, and only carbon dioxide reaches the muscle.
It travels from the alveolus through air tubes straight into the muscle cells, as in insects.
It diffuses into a blood capillary, joins haemoglobin in red blood cells, is carried by the blood (through the heart) to the muscle, then diffuses into muscle cells and enters the mitochondria.
It is carried by white blood cells to the muscle, where it is stored in the cytoplasm and used for protein making.
quiz.rationale: In humans oxygen crosses the alveolar wall into capillaries, binds haemoglobin, is pumped by the heart around the body and diffuses into muscle cells, where mitochondria use it in aerobic respiration. Air tubes carrying gas straight to cells is the insect system.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: Zone C - Gas Exchange Pathway (alveolus to muscle mitochondrion including haemoglobin, blood vessels and heart)

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly shows aerobic respiration of glucose and compares its energy yield with anaerobic respiration in human muscle?
choices: Aerobic: glucose → lactic acid + a large amount of energy. Anaerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + a small amount of energy.
Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + a large amount of energy. Anaerobic: glucose → lactic acid + a small amount of energy.
Both release the same amount of energy, but anaerobic respiration needs oxygen and aerobic respiration does not.
Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + a small amount of energy. Anaerobic: glucose → lactic acid + a large amount of energy.
quiz.rationale: Aerobic respiration completely breaks down glucose using oxygen, giving CO2, water and much more ATP. Anaerobic respiration in animals stops at lactic acid and releases far less energy.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: Zone D - Respiration Equations (aerobic and anaerobic side by side with ATP yield noted)

quiz.prompt: A learner works out the respiratory quotient (RQ) for a Kenyan food example. In an experiment, 160 cm³ of carbon dioxide is produced while 200 cm³ of oxygen is used. What is the RQ?
quiz.rationale: RQ = volume of CO2 produced ÷ volume of O2 used = 160 ÷ 200 = 0.8. Inverting the ratio gives the common wrong answer 1.25.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: Zone D - one worked RQ calculation for a Kenyan food example (ugali, nyama choma or githeri)

quiz.prompt: People living at sea level often find exercise harder when they first go to a high-altitude place in the Rift Valley. What is the best explanation?
choices: At high altitude the enzymes for respiration are denatured by the cold, so respiration stops completely.
The air at high altitude has less oxygen available, so less oxygen reaches the muscle cells and aerobic respiration is limited.
The air at high altitude has more carbon dioxide, which is used by muscle cells instead of oxygen.
The lungs at high altitude cannot move air in and out because the diaphragm stops working.
quiz.rationale: Oxygen availability is a factor affecting respiration rate. At high altitude there is less oxygen in the air, so less is available for aerobic respiration and the body must breathe faster to cope.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: Zone E - Factors Affecting Respiration Rate (oxygen availability with high-altitude Rift Valley example)

quiz.prompt: Why do we often feel thirsty and have a dry mouth after exercise when we breathe hard through the mouth?
choices: The alveoli stop producing fluid when oxygen is scarce.
The lungs produce extra carbon dioxide, which removes water from the mouth.
Air passing through the airways picks up water vapour from the moist lining, so breathing hard loses more water from the body.
Lactic acid made in the muscles dries out the saliva glands.
quiz.rationale: The airways and alveoli keep a thin film of fluid and the air is warmed and moistened as it passes. Hard breathing moves more air, so more water vapour is lost and we feel thirsty.
quiz.placement: DQB phase: closing the question 'Why did our mouths dry out - how does the body keep the alveolus moist?' (posted in Lesson 3)

lessons.title: Summative Review & Transfer: Explaining the Body's Response to Exercise

quiz.prompt: In Lesson 1, a learner who breathed 14 times per minute at rest breathed about 28 times per minute after 2 minutes of step-ups. Which explanation best matches the science learned in this unit?
choices: Learners breathe faster after exercise only because they feel tired
The lungs become smaller during exercise, so they must fill more often
Working muscle cells use more oxygen to make ATP and produce more carbon dioxide, so breathing speeds up to supply oxygen and remove CO₂
The body needs to breathe faster to cool the blood in the lungs
quiz.rationale: Exercise increases ATP demand in muscle cells, so they use more oxygen and release more CO₂. Faster breathing supplies the oxygen and removes the CO₂. 'Because we are tired' is the naive Lesson 1 idea.
quiz.placement: Predict: re-reading the Lesson 1 data table and initial model

quiz.prompt: Which feature of the alveolus makes oxygen diffuse quickly from the air into the blood?
choices: Its thick, waterproof wall that holds the air in
Its wall is only one cell thick, moist, and surrounded by capillaries with a rich blood supply
Its lack of blood vessels, which keeps oxygen in the air sacs
Its small surface area, which concentrates the oxygen
quiz.rationale: A very thin, moist wall, a large surface area and a rich capillary network keep the diffusion distance short and maintain the concentration gradient.
quiz.placement: Observe: Gallery Walk, Evidence Stations 2 and 7 (respiratory surface and alveolus-capillary interface)

quiz.prompt: During inhalation, what happens to the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles?
choices: The diaphragm relaxes and flattens; the intercostal muscles contract so the ribs move down
The diaphragm relaxes and arches upwards; the intercostal muscles relax so the ribs move down
The diaphragm contracts and flattens; the intercostal muscles relax so the ribs move in
The diaphragm contracts and flattens; the intercostal muscles contract and move the ribs up and out
quiz.rationale: On inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the intercostal muscles raise the ribs up and out. Chest volume increases and air pressure falls, so air flows in.
quiz.placement: Observe: Gallery Walk, Evidence Station 3 (diaphragm and intercostal movement observation table and bottle model)

quiz.prompt: Which equation correctly shows aerobic respiration in muscle cells?
choices: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ + 2ATP
6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6CO₂ → 6O₂ + 6H₂O + ATP
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP
quiz.rationale: Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen to produce carbon dioxide, water and ATP. The first equation is lactic acid fermentation and the second is photosynthesis.
quiz.placement: Observe: Gallery Walk, Evidence Station 5 (aerobic respiration equation)

quiz.prompt: A learner writes the Final Explanation component 'The Circulatory Link'. Which statement is scientifically correct?
choices: Blood carries oxygen dissolved only in the plasma, and the heart slows down so the blood has more time to pick it up
In the lungs, haemoglobin in red blood cells combines with oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin, and a faster heart rate carries it more quickly through the capillaries to the muscles
Oxygen travels to the muscles through the windpipe, and blood only carries carbon dioxide away
The heart pumps air from the lungs directly into the muscle cells
quiz.rationale: Haemoglobin picks up oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin. A faster heart rate speeds delivery to muscle capillaries, linking the breathing and circulatory systems.
quiz.placement: Explain: Final Explanation, component 3 (The Circulatory Link)

quiz.prompt: During hard exercise, a learner is breathing very fast but still feels a burning sensation in the leg muscles. What is the best explanation?
choices: Oxygen is not reaching the leg muscle cells fast enough, so some cells break down glucose without oxygen and lactic acid builds up
Fast breathing damages the leg muscles
The muscles have run out of blood, so no respiration is happening
Too much oxygen has reached the muscles and it is burning the muscle tissue
quiz.rationale: When oxygen supply cannot keep up with demand, muscle cells use anaerobic respiration (lactic acid fermentation). The lactic acid accumulates and causes the burning feeling, even though breathing is fast.
quiz.placement: DQB ceremony: Q2 'Why do legs burn even when you are breathing hard?'

quiz.prompt: Akinyi, a swimmer from Kisumu, swims steadily for 8 km, turning to breathe every 3 strokes. Which description best fits her body during this steady swimming?
choices: Her breathing and heart rate increase, blood delivers oxygen on haemoglobin to her muscles, and her muscle cells mainly respire aerobically
Her muscle cells respire only anaerobically, because she holds her breath with her face in the water
Her heart rate falls so that her blood can carry more oxygen
Her breathing rate and heart rate stay the same as at rest because the water cools her
quiz.rationale: Steady exercise raises breathing and heart rate, so enough oxygen reaches the muscles via haemoglobin. The muscle cells mainly use aerobic respiration to make ATP.
quiz.placement: Model Part B: Akinyi transfer task, question 1 (first 8 km of steady swimming)

quiz.prompt: In the last 2 km, Akinyi sprints and her arm muscles burn. Which process and equation describe what is happening in her muscle cells?
choices: Lactic acid fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ + 2ATP, and the burning is caused by lactic acid building up
Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, and the burning is caused by glucose
Lactic acid fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ + 2ATP, and the burning is caused by too much oxygen
Aerobic respiration: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP, and the burning is caused by carbon dioxide
quiz.rationale: When oxygen is insufficient during the sprint, muscle cells use anaerobic respiration (lactic acid fermentation), which releases a small amount of ATP. The lactic acid that accumulates causes the burning sensation.
quiz.placement: Model Part B: Akinyi transfer task, question 2 (final 2 km sprint, process, equation and burning sensation)

quiz.prompt: Akinyi has stopped swimming but is still breathing very heavily. Why?
choices: She is breathing heavily only because she is embarrassed and tired
She is repaying the oxygen debt: the extra oxygen is used to break down the lactic acid that built up and to restore her energy supplies
Her lungs are damaged and cannot slow down
Her muscle cells have stopped respiring and are waiting for oxygen to restart
quiz.rationale: After anaerobic respiration, extra oxygen is needed to oxidise the accumulated lactic acid and to replenish ATP stores. This is the oxygen debt, and it explains the heavy breathing after exercise stops.
quiz.placement: Model Part B: Akinyi transfer task, question 3 (heavy breathing after she stops swimming)
